stories.title: Mamdani Secures Appeals Court Win in Pied-à-Terre Tax Rollout
stories.excerpt: Mayor Zohran Mamdani can move forward with his pied-à-terre tax rollout after a state appellate court Wednesday reversed a lower court’s ruling that the tax’s debut was mishandled. A Staten Island judge ruled in September that the surcharge on luxury second homes in the city unlawfully burdened homeowners with having to prove their residency status, as well as targeted 900,000 residential properties through a public list that included owners’ personal details. Attorney Randy Mastro is representing homeowners in the lawsuit. But Wednesday’s ruling reaffirms the pied-à-terre tax was legal and that property owners did not suffer harm because of the list’s release, which contained details local tax assessors publish regularly. “These public and published assessments contain much of the same information as the supplemental roll at the heart of this appeal,” a panel of appellate judges wrote Wednesday. The pied-à-terre tax, first proposed by Mamdani, was signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul in May and applies to single-family homes worth $5 million or more, as well as co-ops and condos worth at least $1 million. “Today, an appeals court rejected an attempt by the ultra-wealthy to avoid paying their fair share and ruled in favor of the city in a lawsuit challenging the rollout of the pied-à-terre surcharge,” Mamdani said in a statement Wednesday. Meanwhile, Mastro said Wednesday that the appellate court “avoided addressing the merits of this case,” and that he will continue to work on behalf of his plaintiffs. Despite this week’s win, Mamdani isn’t completely out of the woods. Two other lawsuits against the state are arguing the pied-à-terre tax is unconstitutional because it discriminates against non-residents of New York City, according to Bloomberg. Those cases will proceed in December. Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: NY appellate court upheld pied-à-terre tax on homes $5M+, co-ops/condos $1M+ in NYC
Tax applies to luxury second homes; legal challenge over residency disclosure reversed
Removes regulatory uncertainty; tax implementation can proceed without further legal delays
stories.summary: New York's appellate court reversed a lower court ruling and validated the pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes ($5M+ single-family, $1M+ co-ops/condos) after a Staten Island judge had blocked it over residency burden and privacy concerns. The court ruled the tax is legal and that property owners suffered no harm from the public disclosure of owner details. The ruling clears the path for enforcement of the tax signed into law by Gov. Hochul in May.
stories.impact: NYC: Tax creates headwinds for luxury condo/co-op development financing and acquisition pricing, particularly in Manhattan, as investor IRRs compress on high-value properties. Secondary effect: may push capital toward rental multifamily ($1M+ threshold applies to condos/co-ops, not rentals), strengthening demand for apartment development in NYC submarkets as an alternative asset class.

stories.title: Democrats’ Housing Ideas Take Center Stage After Election Rout
stories.excerpt: After a decade of Trump-dominiated politics, Republicans suffered a generational wipeout on Tuesday after rising costs compelled Americans to vote them out of power. By early Wednesday morning, Democrats achieved the unthinkable, flipping seats in deep-red parts of the South, the Midwest and the Great Plains to seize both houses of Congress. As of 2 p.m., Democrats were on track to hold their largest majority since the 2008 election. In the Senate, Democrats controlled 54 seats so far, adding seven while emerging slightly ahead in two too-close-to-call races in Alaska and Mississippi. New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, who will likely lead the Senate next year, called the results a “generational remake of the Senate majority” and told reporters the first thing he would do is “reduce people’s costs and work the legislative process so it does.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in position to become the first Black House speaker in the nation’s history, said his party’s mission will be to lower the cost of living instead of prioritizing retribution against Republicans. “We made clear that we’re fighting for an affordable America and explicitly promised the American people that we would fight hard to lower the high costs of groceries, gas and housing,” Jeffries, whose district encompasses a lot of Brooklyn, told MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday. “Hardworking American taxpayers who are working hard and playing by the rules should be able to live an affordable life.” President Donald Trump promised to reduce the cost of living while taming inflation when he ran two years ago. Instead, prices rose. Nearly half of Americans at the start of this year did not have the resources to cover their basic expenses and meet their needs, according to an Urban Institute study. bullets: Democrats flipped both houses of Congress; Schumer will lead Senate, Jeffries poised as Speaker
Democratic majority focused on 'reducing people's costs' as core legislative agenda
Policy shift signals potential for housing-supply-focused legislation and cost-control initiatives
stories.summary: Democrats achieved a landslide victory in Tuesday's election, securing majorities in both houses of Congress. New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, positioned to lead the Senate, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become the first Black House Speaker, both emphasized cost reduction as their immediate legislative priority. Democrats will hold their largest Senate majority since 2008 (54 seats and leading in two races).
stories.impact: NATIONAL: Democratic control and focus on affordability/cost reduction may accelerate pro-housing-supply legislation (zoning reform, streamlined entitlements, financing incentives), but could also trigger rent regulation or inclusionary-zoning mandates—both outcomes affect underwriting assumptions and feasibility in regulated markets like NYC, CA, and major metros. Developers should monitor committee assignments and early housing bills for capital and cost implications.

stories.title: Commercial Real Estate Distress Heading for Moment of Truth
stories.excerpt: Commercial Observer’s annual fall National Finance Forum held the morning of Election Day had the feel of a calm before the storm. Some of commercial real estate’s biggest players spoke at the semiannual event, held at Quorum by Convene at 1221 Avenue of the Americas, stressed that while the near future should present plenty of compelling deal opportunities, some historic distress levels also may be on the horizon. “We think there is big distress coming, and I think everybody in this room is sensing it with where [interest] rates are and what it does to cap rates,” Ran Eliasaf, founder and managing partner of Northwind Group, said during the symposium’s opening session. Eliasaf predicted rising interest rates and their compounding negative effect on cap rates will lead to major stress on the CRE market that could rival the 2008 Global Financial Crisis period. “You go outside in New York City and leasing velocity and rents are declining, even in multifamily, and I think in many deals that were done the last five years, the capital stacks were upside down,” Eliasaf said. “There is a chance, I don’t know the probability of it, but we’re going to see a huge correction and huge distress even in balance sheets of CLO lenders and banks. It could be as large as 2008. Maybe it’s not, but we’re very concerned.” Eliasaf spoke during the first session called Opening Real Estate Credit Market Report. The session also featured Michael Ainbinder, partner and head of CRE credit at Northwind Group, and moderator Brian Steinwurtzel, CEO and principal of GFP Development. The distress facing the CRE markets could be especially pronounced in the multifamily sector, according to Larry Kravetz, managing director, head of U.S. CRE and CMBS at Nomura Securities, who spoke in the opening keynote. bullets: CRE distress predicted by major players; rising rates driving cap-rate compression and deal stress
NYC multifamily leasing velocity and rents declining; capital stacks 'upside down' on recent deals
2008-scale distress expected; lenders tightening amid negative market fundamentals across sectors
stories.summary: Speaking at Commercial Observer's National Finance Forum on Election Day, Ran Eliasaf of Northwind Group predicted historic commercial real estate distress comparable to 2008, driven by rising interest rates and cap-rate compression. He noted that NYC multifamily specifically shows declining leasing velocity and rents, with many deals from the past five years carrying inverted capital stacks. Lenders are tightening underwriting in response to deteriorating market conditions.
stories.impact: NYC & NATIONAL: Rising rates are compressing valuations and forcing refinancing stress on stabilized multifamily assets; deals underwritten at low rates now face negative arbitrage. Window of opportunity for accretive acquisitions of distressed assets at reduced prices; however, developers must secure permanent financing before rates stabilize. Downside: starts may decelerate as development-stage projects struggle to pencil with higher debt costs and softening rents.

stories.title: Catalyst IOS Expands Midtown Headquarters Space
stories.excerpt: Catalyst IOS, a leading operator of industrial outdoor storage (IOS) properties in high-barrier-to-entry urban infill markets, has signed a full-floor, 12,000-square-foot lease to expand its headquarters on the 35th floor of SL Green’s 800 Third Ave. in Midtown Manhattan. The five-year lease doubles the size of Catalyst’s current 6,000-square-foot office space on the 27th floor of the building. The office expansion comes as Catalyst continues to scale its dedicated IOS platform, which currently comprises over $1.4 billion in AUM across over 220 properties across the U.S. “Catalyst has been an exemplary tenant with a strong prospect for future growth. Their management team is proactive and highly regarded,” said Steven Durels, EVP and director of leasing and real property for SL Green “We look forward to partnering with them as they continue to expand their business.” SL Green was represented by Harry Blair, Kyle Cohen and Kelli Berke of Cushman & Wakefield. The Catalyst IOS team plans to fully take occupancy of the space later in the fourth quarter. The post Catalyst IOS Expands Midtown Headquarters Space appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Catalyst IOS expands Midtown Manhattan HQ from 6K to 12K sq ft on 5-year lease
Signals confidence in NYC office; IOS platform managing $1.4B AUM across 220+ properties
Reflects selective office recovery for specialized/growth operators despite broader CRE headwinds
stories.summary: Catalyst IOS, an operator of industrial outdoor storage properties, signed a full-floor, 12,000-square-foot lease to double its headquarters space at SL Green's 800 Third Ave. in Midtown Manhattan for five years. The expansion follows the company's scaling of its $1.4 billion AUM platform across 220+ U.S. properties. SL Green represented the landlord; IPA Capital Markets will arrange financing.
stories.impact: MINIMAL TO MULTIFAMILY: Office tenant expansion reflects confidence in Catalyst's niche IOS platform but does not signal demand for rental housing or shift in Manhattan residential fundamentals. Note: SL Green's willingness to lease suggests selective recovery in Midtown office for well-capitalized, growth-stage operators; however, this is not a broad market-level signal for residential development.

stories.title: Benedict Canyon Acquires Neighboring West Hollywood Properties
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap completed the sale and financing of 884 and 939 Palm Ave., two multifamily properties totaling 72 units in West Hollywood. The assets traded for $29.85 million, or $414,583 per unit. Tony Azzi and Rabbie Banafsheha of The Azzi Group of Marcus & Millichap exclusively represented the seller, a private family investor. Azzi, Banafsheha, Arteen Zahiri and Ian Habbestad of The Azzi Group also procured the buyer, Benedict Canyon Equities, a Southern California-based multifamily investment firm that has acquired more than 13,700 apartment units. Jake Vitta, Brian Eisendrath, and Cameron Chalfant of IPA Capital Markets arranged acquisition financing on behalf of the buyer. Azzi said, “West Hollywood consistently experiences high tenant demand driven by limited housing supply, walkability, and access to major employment hubs throughout the Westside and Hollywood. Opportunities to acquire 72 units on Palm Avenue in a single transaction are exceptionally rare and these are irreplaceable assets in a market where new supply is effectively constrained.” Built in 1990, 939 Palm Ave. is a four-story, 42-unit building, and 884 Palm Avenue, completed in 1989, is a three-story, 30-unit building. Both properties feature subterranean parking, fitness centers, swimming pools, spas, and large private decks. The post Benedict Canyon Acquires Neighboring West Hollywood Properties appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Benedict Canyon acquires 72-unit portfolio (884 & 939 Palm Ave) in West Hollywood for $29.85M
Per-unit price: $414,583; limited supply, high tenant demand, walkability, constrained new supply noted
Consolidation play in supply-constrained submarket; irreplaceable assets capturing West LA employment hub access
stories.summary: Benedict Canyon Equities acquired two multifamily properties totaling 72 units in West Hollywood for $29.85 million, or approximately $414,583 per unit. The assets—939 Palm Ave. (42 units, built 1990) and 884 Palm Ave. (30 units, built 1989)—traded in a rare single-transaction opportunity. Marcus & Millichap's Azzi Group highlighted West Hollywood's limited new supply, high tenant demand, walkability, and proximity to Westside and Hollywood employment as value drivers.
stories.impact: LOS ANGELES (West Hollywood/Westside): Price per unit and broker commentary underscore severe supply constraints—new development is effectively blocked by zoning/entitlements. Strong rental demand from Westside employment anchors (tech, entertainment, services) supports rent growth and acquisition interest. Implication for developers: ground-up multifamily in West Hollywood is difficult; acquisition/hold/value-add is preferred path. Land control/zoning certainty essential before acquisition in this submarket.

stories.title: JLL Arranges Refi for Mixed-Use Residential on Long Island’s South Shore
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged a $154.25-million refinancing for Greybarn Amityville, a mixed-use residential property in Amityville, NY, owned by Rechler Equity Partners. Senior managing directors Peter Rotchford and Andrew Scandalios and director Clayton Ross arranged the financing through PCCP, LLC. “Lenders are looking closely at how a multifamily property performs today and at the owner’s ability to keep it competitive over time,” said Rotchford. “Greybarn brought together established residential demand, a strong amenity offering and an owner that developed and continues to manage the property, all factors that helped us secure substantial financing in a market where lenders remain selective.” Developed by Rechler in three phases between 2016 and 2020, Greybarn is located at 805 Broadway in Amityville on Long Island’s South Shore. It features 335 apartments and 37,737 square feet of ground-floor retail space. It’s a fully stabilized property in a market with limited new construction. The post JLL Arranges Refi for Mixed-Use Residential on Long Island’s South Shore appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JLL arranged $154.25M refi for Greybarn Amityville (335 units + 37.7K SF retail) via PCCP
Fully stabilized; developed 2016–2020; strong owner track record and amenities enabled financing in selective market
Lender focus on current performance and competitive positioning in limited-supply market
stories.summary: JLL Capital Markets arranged a $154.25 million refinancing for Greybarn Amityville, a mixed-use property owned by Rechler Equity Partners featuring 335 apartments and 37,737 square feet of ground-floor retail. Developed in three phases between 2016 and 2020, the property is fully stabilized in a market with limited new construction. Senior managing directors Peter Rotchford and Andrew Scandalios highlighted the owner's development/management track record and strong amenity offering as key factors in securing financing in a selective lending environment.
stories.impact: LONG ISLAND (Amityville/South Shore): Lenders remain selective and focused on demonstrated owner competency, current operational performance, and market scarcity. Refi at $154.25M on 335 units (~$460K/unit debt) in a stabilized, limited-supply market signals lender appetite for quality, proven-operator assets. Takeaway: ground-up development on Long Island must emphasize owner/operator pedigree and pre-leasing/demand evidence to attract capital in current environment.

stories.title: Erland Completes Athletic Field House for Middlesex School
stories.excerpt: Erland Construction, in collaboration with Rimkus and CBT Architects, has completed the Curtis Center, a new athletic field house at Middlesex School on the school’s historic Concord campus. The new two-story, 106,000-square-foot facility was designed and constructed to support a wide range of programs and activities. The field house features a fitness center, indoor turf practice space, two basketball/volleyball courts, an elevated indoor track, and lower-level parking for 72 vehicles. The building is also expected to achieve LEED Silver certification. Ben McConchie, academic group manager at Erland Construction, said, “Projects like this are about more than just the building. They’re about the experience it creates for students every day. From early-morning practices to team events and informal use, this facility will be in constant use. It’s rewarding to see how it’s already becoming a central part of campus life, and we’re proud to have played a role in delivering it.” The post Erland Completes Athletic Field House for Middlesex School appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Erland Construction completed 106K SF athletic field house (Curtis Center) for Middlesex School in Concord, MA
Mixed-use facility: fitness center, indoor turf, courts, track, parking; targeting LEED Silver
Non-multifamily; institutional/educational construction project with no direct housing impact
stories.summary: Erland Construction, in collaboration with Rimkus and CBT Architects, completed the Curtis Center, a 106,000-square-foot athletic field house for Middlesex School's Concord campus. The two-story facility includes a fitness center, indoor turf practice space, two basketball/volleyball courts, an elevated indoor track, and parking for 72 vehicles, and is targeting LEED Silver certification.
stories.impact: NOT RELEVANT TO MULTIFAMILY DEVELOPMENT: This is an institutional/educational construction project with no impact on residential housing supply, demand, or capital markets in any major multifamily metro.

stories.title: Dunleer Trades Huntington Beach Industrial in Off-Market Sale
stories.excerpt: Dunleer, a Los Angeles-based private real estate investment and development firm, closed the $8.23-million sale of Talbert Industrial Park, a newly renovated, two-building small-bay industrial property located at 7602 Talbert Ave. in Huntington Beach. The 22,383-square-foot property was sold off market for approximately $367 per square foot, one of the highest per-square-foot prices for comparable Huntington Beach industrial assets. “After acquiring the property in 2024, Dunleer immediately implemented a value-add strategy focused on enhancing functionality, improving the tenant experience and maximizing the property’s appeal,” said BJ Turner, CEO of Dunleer. “This is an incredibly well-located asset, and it is very difficult to find industrial properties west of the 405 in prime Orange County. With an average annual household income above $145,000 within a five-mile radius, it’s one of Southern California’s most desirable multi-tenant industrial locations.” Carter Hadley and Alexander Harrold of Matthews Real Estate Investment Services represented Dunleer. The buyer was a private investor based in San Diego. The post Dunleer Trades Huntington Beach Industrial in Off-Market Sale appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Dunleer closed $8.23M off-market sale of 22,383 SF industrial in Huntington Beach (Talbert Ave)
Price: ~$367/SF; smallest comparable industrial west of 405 in Orange County; high-income demographic
Supply-constrained Orange County industrial location; value-add strategy demonstrating execution risk/reward cycle
stories.summary: Dunleer, a Los Angeles-based developer, sold the Talbert Industrial Park, a newly renovated two-building small-bay industrial property (22,383 SF) in Huntington Beach for $8.23 million, or approximately $367 per square foot. Dunleer acquired the property in 2024, implemented a value-add strategy, and sold off-market to a San Diego private investor. The broker noted the per-square-foot price represents one of the highest for comparable Huntington Beach industrial assets.
stories.impact: MINIMAL TO MULTIFAMILY: Industrial transaction in Orange County; no direct housing impact. Secondary note: high per-SF price and supply scarcity west of I-405 suggest limited development land availability in Orange County—if industrial is constrained, multifamily land is even scarcer, reinforcing pricing power in existing rental communities and difficulty in ground-up development pipeline.

stories.title: NYC Ballot Proposals Passed in Tuesday’s Election to Go Into Effect
stories.excerpt: New York City voters approved Tuesday five ballot proposals crafted by Mamdani administration appointees to speed up development and give restaurants more leeway in serving food and drink outdoors. While the post-election focus has been on the landslide to the left in states such as Texas, Kansas and Georgia, commercial real estate developers and operators in New York City will see some benefits from more efficient processes for approving outdoor dining and a centralized processing center for some construction projects. Most of the outdoor dining change goes into effect March 1, those pertaining to sales and waterfront construction will be made effective Dec. 31, 2030. Mitchell Korbey, partner and chair of the land use and zoning group at Herrick, was particularly enthusiastic about Proposals 3 and 4. The measures are designed to speed up safety reviews, fast-track the sale of city-owned land, simplify the construction permit process, and otherwise remove speed bumps on the road to development. “This will unlock opportunities that otherwise take considerable time given the current requirement for uniform land use review procedure (ULURP),” Korbey said. “For Proposal 4, shifting authority to the Department of Buildings (DOB) represents a far more efficient process and more expert and logical method for reviewing — resulting in time savings and greater predictability.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani launched an individual campaign to get the word out on these proposals in September after the commission approved them in July. “New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do,” Mamdani said in a statement Tuesday night. “From opening outdoor dining faster to speeding up street safety projects to accelerating housing production, we are cutting red tape that will directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love. Now comes the work of turning these votes into results.” Proposal 1 aims to speed up the process for using public s
bullets: NYC voters approved 5 ballot measures to streamline development approvals and outdoor dining rules
Proposals 3 & 4 fast-track construction permits, city-land sales, and safety reviews; effective Dec 31, 2030
Outdoor dining changes effective March 1; centralized permitting center removes procedural delays on residential/mixed-use projects
stories.summary: New York City voters approved five ballot measures Tuesday designed to accelerate development and ease outdoor dining regulations. Proposals 3 and 4 streamline construction safety reviews, fast-track sales of city-owned land, and simplify permit processing. Outdoor dining changes take effect March 1; sales and waterfront construction rules become effective December 31, 2030. Herrick LLP's Mitchell Korbey noted the measures remove significant procedural delays for developers and operators.
stories.impact: NYC: Permitting acceleration and centralized processing lower soft costs and development timeline for residential and mixed-use projects; improved feasibility for mid-size developers. City-owned-land fast-track (effective Dec. 31, 2030) could unlock several development sites in outer boroughs and waterfront, increasing competitive land supply and moderating acquisition pricing. Immediate impact on outdoor dining may support mixed-use retail leasing in rental communities with ground-floor activation.

stories.title: GridPoint Co-Founder Adrian De Luca Returns as CEO to Power New Battery Product
stories.excerpt: GridPoint, an energy data management platform for commercial real estate, announced Wednesday that co-founder Adrian De Luca has returned to the company as CEO to lead the rollout of its new storage battery business. The company said it plans to add on-site storage batteries across its platform of more than 20,000 commercial sites in the United States, targeting a total of 2 gigawatts of distributed storage capacity, which it calls equivalent to the entire generating capacity of the Hoover Dam. De Luca rejoins the company from I Squared Capital, where he was a principal at the global infrastructure investment firm that has $60 billion in assets under management. “Our mission for the last 20 years has been very simple: We have been deploying our energy management technology to multi-site retail operators to drive two key business outcomes at the highest level,” said De Luca. “The first one is energy efficiency — using technology to drive down the energy spend for these businesses and to do it reliably across formats, markets and operating models. And the second key business outcome is operational efficiency.” De Luca’s return and the product rollout come as U.S. electricity demand is on track to set records in 2026 and 2027, according to a July 2026 U.S. Energy Information Administration report. The demand is largely driven by growth in data centers and advanced manufacturing. That pressure is evident in rapidly rising operating costs for businesses managing thousands of restaurants, pharmacies, retail locations and other facilities, as commercial electricity rates rose 42 percent across GridPoint sites over the past five years, the company said. “My role prior to this was as an investor and a board adviser,” De Luca said of his path to returning to GridPoint. “So I’ve been around the company for a long time, going all the way back to the founding team that I was a part of in late 2003. bullets: GridPoint co-founder Adrian De Luca returns as CEO to scale on-site battery storage business
Target: 2 GW distributed storage capacity across 20K+ CRE sites; positioned as grid-resilience solution
Battery storage increasingly embedded in multifamily developments for resilience, efficiency, and operational savings
stories.summary: GridPoint announced that co-founder Adrian De Luca has returned as CEO to lead rollout of the company's new on-site storage battery business. The company plans to deploy storage batteries across its platform of 20,000+ commercial sites, targeting 2 gigawatts of distributed storage capacity. De Luca previously worked at I Squared Capital, a $60 billion global infrastructure investment firm. GridPoint's focus is energy efficiency and operational efficiency for multi-site operators.
stories.impact: NATIONAL: Growing adoption of on-site battery storage in CRE, including multifamily, driven by grid resilience, energy cost reduction, and operational efficiency. Developers incorporating battery+solar or grid-interactive systems in new apartments can command higher rents, lower tenant energy costs, and attract institutional capital focused on ESG/operational risk mitigation. Capital cost of batteries declining; integration into multifamily mixed-use projects increasingly feasible and market-competitive.
